description: No ethics committee, IRB, or institutional approval is mentioned. The study or tool proceeds without documented ethics oversight.
An ethics committee, IRB process, or institutional approval is explicitly mentioned or obtained.
A specific ethics committee or review board is named or referenced.
No consent mechanism exists. Attackers or affected parties are not informed or given any form of consent.
Attackers are treated as implicitly consenting adversaries with no active consent mechanism; assumes hostile intent.
Explicit informed consent is obtained from participants or parties interacting with the honeypot.
The system includes or discusses notifying attackers that they are interacting with a honeypot.
Users or operators of the monitored network are not notified about honeypot deployment.
The honeypot captures attacker usernames and/or passwords in plaintext or encoded form.
Full attacker sessions are recorded, including keystrokes, commands, screenshots, or terminal activity.
Malware binaries or exploit payloads are captured and stored by the honeypot.
Full or partial network traffic (pcap) is captured from attacker interactions.
Attacker IP addresses are systematically logged and retained as identifiers.
Data collected may constitute personal data under privacy regulations (e.g., email addresses, device identifiers, Bluetooth MACs).
ICS/SCADA-specific protocol data (Modbus, S7comm, DNP3, BACnet, etc.) is captured from attacker interactions.
Interaction data may include or reference medical identifiers (DICOM patient IDs, HL7/FHIR patient records).
Attacker behavioral patterns, command sequences, or interaction profiles are collected and analyzed.
No data retention policy, deletion timeline, or archival strategy is documented.
A data retention policy or deletion schedule is explicitly mentioned.
No discussion of data minimization, selective logging, or privacy filtering is present.
Data minimization principles are explicitly applied or discussed.
Captured attack data or datasets are publicly released without restrictions.
Captured data is shared in a controlled manner (e.g., requires application, institutional affiliation, or review).
Attack data is automatically or semi-automatically submitted to a third-party platform or service.
No dataset, logs, or attack data are shared beyond the immediate research team.
The honeypot deployment creates a risk of capturing or exposing personal or sensitive private data.
The data collection practices may trigger GDPR or similar data protection regulation obligations, not discussed.
Attacker IP addresses are collected without anonymization, raising privacy concerns under data protection law.
The honeypot is deployed on or distributed to consumer-facing devices (e.g., mobile apps, Play Store), raising end-user privacy concerns.
No legal framework, jurisdiction analysis, or regulatory compliance is discussed.
Legal jurisdiction, applicable laws, or regulatory compliance is explicitly addressed.
The honeypot operates on regulated radio frequencies, raising spectrum regulatory compliance concerns not discussed.
The honeypot design or deployment may raise questions about legal entrapment of attackers.
Terms of service, copyright, or acceptable use policy concerns arise from the honeypot design (e.g., website cloning).
Containment is achieved passively through logging only; the honeypot does not actively engage or respond to attacker infrastructure.
Active containment measures are implemented (e.g., containerization, network isolation, VM sandboxing, namespace isolation).
No containment or harm prevention measures are documented.
A specific containment gap or risk is identified (e.g., proxy to real backend, malware escape risk, real device exposure).
The honeypot proxies to or connects with a real backend system, creating risk of real data exposure to attackers.
A compromised or weaponized honeypot could be used to attack third parties; this risk is not addressed.
Honeypot deployment in or near physical systems (ICS, medical devices, spacecraft, radio) creates risk of physical harm.
Deception is framed purely as an engineering or security mechanism with no ethical analysis or moral reasoning.
The ethical dimensions of using deception against attackers are explicitly discussed or reasoned about.
The honeypot actively transmits deceptive signals, responses, or content (beyond passive emulation).
Deception extends beyond cyber into the physical world (fake video feeds, simulated physical processes, radio signals).
Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to generate dynamic, realistic deceptive responses to attackers.
The honeypot design, code, or data could be misused by attackers to evade detection, test attack tools, or cause harm.
No statements about researcher responsibility, ethical guidelines, or professional conduct are present.
Researcher responsibility, ethical obligations, or professional guidelines are explicitly stated.
Responsible disclosure of vulnerabilities, attacker identities, or threat intelligence is discussed.
The authors acknowledge the dual-use potential of the honeypot design or published findings.
Attacker interaction data is transmitted to a third-party LLM API (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) for processing, without documented governance.
AI-powered honeypot components operate without any documented AI-specific governance, bias assessment, or accountability framework.
The honeypot generates automated responses to attackers (scripted or AI-driven) without human review of each response.
Technical capabilities (AI, digital twins, high-fidelity simulation) advance faster than the accompanying ethical governance framework.
The honeypot is deployed on publicly accessible infrastructure facing real internet attackers.
The honeypot is deployed in a controlled lab, testbed, or experimental environment rather than against live attacker traffic.
The honeypot operates in a simulated environment with no real-world attacker exposure.
The honeypot is deployed in or adjacent to critical infrastructure (power grid, water treatment, transportation, telecommunications, space).
The honeypot or sensor is distributed directly to general consumers (e.g., via app stores, public downloads).
The honeypot is deployed on mobile devices carried into real-world environments.
Captured attack data is contributed to a threat intelligence platform or community feed.
Threat intelligence is shared without documented anonymization, access control, or privacy policy.
Data collected from or about non-attacker parties (victims, legitimate users, infrastructure operators) is captured without consent.
Ethical compliance is implicitly assumed to be achieved through technical containment (isolation, sandboxing) rather than normative ethical reasoning.
No ethical framing, discussion, or reasoning is present in the document at all.
Some ethical concepts are mentioned but not developed into a full ethical analysis or governance framework.
Specific ethical concerns arising from honeypot deployment in Industrial Control System environments (safety, critical infrastructure, cascading failure risk).
Specific ethical concerns arising from honeypot deployment involving healthcare data or medical infrastructure (HIPAA, patient privacy, safety).
Specific ethical concerns arising from honeypot deployment in space or satellite system contexts.
Specific ethical concerns arising from honeypot deployment targeting IoT devices or embedded systems at scale.
